about: Written by tools/build_moma_influence.mjs from the MoMA Influence Map study (moma-money-map.html). Text only; the network drawing is not copied.

museum.note: Reported government grants: $49,965 (FY2020), $20,000 (FY2021), $10.0M (FY2022, federal SVOG), none (FY2023, FY2024).

entries.name: City of New York
entries.role: Capital funder; three ex officio board seats
entries.note: The City put $65M into the $650M Taniguchi expansion (opened 2004). The Mayor, Council Speaker and Comptroller sit ex officio on MoMA's board. MoMA gets no city operating subsidy; it is not in the Cultural Institutions Group.

entries.name: Trust for Cultural Resources
entries.role: NY State public-benefit corporation; conduit bond issuer
entries.note: Issued tax-exempt Series 1996, 2000 ($75.75M), 2001 ($235M) and 2016-One-E ($278.4M par) bonds for MoMA. Also administers the Museum Tower tax-equivalency scheme.

entries.name: Museum Tower TEPs
entries.role: Property-tax diversion under NY Arts & Cultural Affairs Law
entries.note: The condo tower above MoMA pays no property tax. The Trust collects equivalent payments and routes them to the City, then bond service, then back to MoMA, which advanced $45M between 1980 and 2000.

entries.name: US Small Business Administration
entries.note: MoMA's only large federal grant on record; disclosed as a subsequent event in the FY2021 audited statements and as government grants on the FY2022 Form 990. No PPP loan appears in any filing.

entries.name: National Endowment for the Arts
entries.note: USAspending shows three NEA grants (film preservation, architecture) in 2008–09. MoMA carries a "National Endowment for the Arts Endowment Fund" from earlier challenge grants.

entries.name: NYC Dept. of Cultural Affairs
entries.role: Ex officio on the MoMA PS1 board; PS1 is a CIG member since 1982
entries.note: The Commissioner, the Queens Borough President and the 26th District Council Member sit on the PS1 board.

entries.name: Other foreign cultural agencies
entries.note: Consulates of Brazil and Spain, Government of Flanders, Japan Foundation, Taiwan Ministry of Culture, Ministério da Cultura do Brasil, Institut Ramon Llull, Pro Helvetia, French Embassy (PS1).

entries.name: Sharon Percy Rockefeller
entries.role: Trustee; President of The International Council
entries.note: Spouse of former Senator Jay Rockefeller; daughter of Senator Charles Percy.

entries.name: Laurence D. Fink
entries.note: Sat on Trump's Strategic and Policy Forum in 2017. Targeted by Strike MoMA in 2021 for that and for BlackRock's holdings.

entries.name: BlackRock
entries.role: Corporate member; the world's largest asset manager ($15.3T, June 2026), not a hedge fund
entries.money: $25,000 tier FY2019–FY2025; $250,000 lead gift, 2016 award luncheon honoring Fink
entries.note: Hired by the Federal Reserve in March 2020 to run its corporate-credit purchase facilities. Full list of investment firms under Directory.

entries.name: Federal Reserve
entries.note: BlackRock's Financial Markets Advisory unit managed the purchases.

entries.name: HHS · BARDA · Operation Warp Speed
entries.role: Federal buyer of MoMA members' products
entries.money: $1.95B Pfizer · $1B J&J · $450M Regeneron · up to $629M SIGA
entries.note: The secondary link between MoMA's pharma members and Washington: the 2020 vaccine and antibody purchase agreements, and BARDA's smallpox-antiviral stockpile contracts with SIGA.

entries.name: US State Department
entries.note: John Hay Whitney (UK, 1957–61), William A. M. Burden (Belgium, 1959–61), Ronald Lauder (Austria, 1986–87). Nelson Rockefeller was Assistant Secretary of State for Latin America, 1944–45. René d'Harnoncourt sat on the Department's Advisory Committee on Art.

entries.name: Pfizer Inc.
entries.role: Corporate member every sampled year since FY2016
entries.note: Leader level in 2018; $25k tier FY2019–FY2025. Employee matching gifts too.

entries.name: Albert Bourla · David Rockefeller Award 2021
entries.note: MoMA honored Pfizer's CEO "accepting on behalf of Pfizer Inc." in a virtual conversation with Marie-Josée Kravis. The event funds MoMA's Department of Education.

entries.name: Roche (Hoffmann-La Roche)
entries.note: The founding family pool holds a majority of Roche voting shares.

entries.name: Maja Oeri
entries.note: Great-granddaughter of the Roche founder; about 7.5% of Roche voting equity. Major gifts to the collection; a permanent-collection gallery is named for her and Hans Bodenmann.

entries.name: Jon Stryker
entries.note: Heir to Stryker Corporation (orthopaedics and medical devices).

entries.name: Regeneron · Merck · BMS · Lilly · Vertex
entries.note: These companies appear only in the Matching Gifts list, meaning they matched an employee's personal gift.

entries.name: Jillian Sackler
entries.note: Widow of Arthur M. Sackler, who died in 1987 before Purdue launched OxyContin. No Sackler-named space or board role at MoMA.

entries.name: Ronald O. Perelman
entries.note: Republican donor. Controls SIGA Technologies, whose smallpox antiviral TPOXX is sold to the US national stockpile.

entries.name: Trump administration & 2017 inaugural
entries.role: Where MoMA's donors and the executive branch meet
entries.money: $1M each from Henry Kravis, Steven Cohen and Len Blavatnik to the inaugural
entries.note: Larry Fink and Stephen Schwarzman sat on the 2017 Strategic and Policy Forum (Schwarzman chaired it). John Paulson was a campaign economic adviser. Ronald Lauder is a long-time friend and donor.

entries.name: Senate & Congressional Leadership Funds
entries.note: Steven Cohen is the top individual donor to both. Ken Griffin has given about $78M to these and allied Republican groups. Steven Tananbaum gives to GOP committees.

entries.name: Ronald S. Lauder
entries.note: Reagan's Ambassador to Austria; 1989 Republican mayoral candidate ($13.6M self-funded); Trump friend and donor in 2016 and 2020; $1M to the Republican State Leadership Committee in 2022. Forbes puts his lifetime political spend above $70M. Mentioned more than 900 times in the January 2026 DOJ Epstein files, including a 2014 email sending Epstein the possession and loan agreement for a Kurt Schwitters work he co-owns with Leon Black; in 2017 their assistants arranged meetings and calls. ARTnews found no direct communication between the two men; Lauder has not commented.

entries.name: Marie-Josée Kravis
entries.role: Chair of the Board since 2021; President 2005–2018
entries.note: Vice Chair of the Hudson Institute; former executive director of the Hudson Institute of Canada.

entries.name: Henry R. Kravis
entries.role: Kravis Studio and chief-curator chair namesake
entries.note: $1M to Trump's 2017 inaugural; $300,000+ to the RNC in 2016. KKR co-founder.

entries.name: Sid R. Bass
entries.note: Texas Bass family, long-time Republican donors.

entries.name: Steven A. Cohen
entries.note: Republican-only donor since 2010 per Artnet; top individual donor to the Senate Leadership Fund and Congressional Leadership Fund.

entries.name: Steven Tananbaum
entries.note: About $250,000 to GOP committees since 2019, including JD Vance's 2022 Senate run. GoldenTree founder.

entries.name: Leon D. Black
entries.note: Mostly Republican giving. Paid Epstein $158M–$170M for tax and estate advice (2012–17); stepped down as Chair in 2021 but remains a trustee. A New York Times investigation (October 2025) of emails showed Epstein structuring Black's art transactions for tax purposes, including around the $120M purchase of Munch's "The Scream"; Black's lawyer says the fees were for legitimate advice. Subject of a Senate Finance Committee inquiry; named in the January 2026 DOJ release; testified to House Oversight in June 2026. DOJ files show Epstein guided his $115M purchase of Picasso's "Buste de Femme (Marie-Thérèse)" from Gagosian, a sculpture shown in MoMA's 2015 "Picasso Sculpture". In 2023 he paid the US Virgin Islands $62.5M to settle Epstein-related claims; the settlement notes he was not accused of wrongdoing. He also funds Bard College, Dartmouth's Black Family Visual Arts Center, Harvard's Poetry in America and the Neue Galerie (Leaving it on the table).

entries.name: Maurice R. Greenberg
entries.note: Former AIG chief; gave via C.V. Starr & Co.

entries.name: Kenneth C. Griffin
entries.role: East Wing namesake ($40M, 2015); Annual Exhibition Fund donor FY2021–FY2025
entries.note: He also funds Lincoln Center, M+ (Hong Kong), the National Gallery (London), National Gallery Singapore, Pérez Art Museum Miami, The Bass and the Whitney (Leaving it on the table); activists targeted him at the Whitney in 2023, not at MoMA. DeSantis's largest donor; third-largest donor of the 2022 midterms. His ex-spouse Anne Dias Griffin is a trustee.

entries.name: Helen Zell
entries.note: Widow of Sam Zell, a major Republican donor.

entries.name: Murdoch family · News Corp
entries.role: Owner of two MoMA corporate members

entries.name: Paulson & Co. (John Paulson)
entries.note: John Paulson was a Trump economic adviser and donor.

entries.name: Schwarzman · Langone · Blavatnik · Loeb · Tepper
entries.note: Christine and Stephen Schwarzman ($50k–$99k, FY2016), Elaine and Ken Langone ($25k, FY2016), Blavatnik Family Foundation ($25k, FY2019), Margaret and Daniel Loeb ($10k–$15k), Appaloosa LP ($10k, FY2016).

entries.name: Jeffrey Epstein
entries.role: Financier; convicted sex offender (2008); died in federal custody 2019
entries.note: Two current MoMA trustees had long financial or personal relationships with him. He was never a MoMA donor or board member on any record found; a similarly named foundation in MoMA's lists (Epstein Teicher Philanthropies) is an unrelated Teicher-family fund founded in 1977.

entries.name: Glenn Dubin
entries.note: Family friend of Epstein since the 1980s; the Dubins appear in Epstein's pilot logs at least 18 times between 1996 and 2005. Epstein invested in Highbridge Capital, Dubin's firm, saying in a 2011 deposition that his stake grew from $50M–$100M to more than $300M; Dubin's representatives say it was far smaller and fully withdrawn. Virginia Giuffre named him in a 2015 filing; he has categorically denied it and says flight records disprove it. Subpoenaed by the US Virgin Islands in 2020 and named in documents unsealed in January 2024. The New York Post reported in October 2019 that MoMA had named a fourth-floor gallery after him and his wife.

entries.name: Eva Andersson-Dubin
entries.note: Dated Epstein in the early 1980s and stayed close to him. Bloomberg (February 2026) reported from the files that she introduced Epstein to hedge-fund managers as late as 2016 and that the correspondence ran until shortly before his death; Mount Sinai opened a review of her Epstein ties in March 2026.

entries.name: Dechert review (Jan 2021)
entries.role: Independent review commissioned by Apollo's board
entries.note: Found the payments were for tax and estate advice and found no wrongdoing by Black. Black stepped down as Apollo CEO in March 2021 and did not seek re-election as MoMA Chair; his chairmanship ended 1 July 2021.

entries.name: US Virgin Islands Attorney General
entries.role: Civil enforcement against the Epstein estate
entries.note: Subpoenaed Black and Dubin in 2020 for Epstein-related records. Black's settlement released him from future USVI claims.

entries.name: Senate Finance Committee (Sen. Wyden)
entries.role: Investigation of Epstein's finances, including Black's payments, 2023–26; Wyden as Chair to January 2025, then Ranking Member
entries.note: Wyden unveiled the inquiry in July 2023, asked the IRS in July 2025 why the transactions were never audited (putting the payments at $170M), and wrote to Black again in March 2026 over what the files suggest were "hush money" payments and surveillance of women. An August 2026 committee report turned to the banks that handled Epstein's money.

entries.name: DOJ Epstein files (2025–26)
entries.role: Justice Department releases: February 2025 (pilot flight logs), December 2025 and 30 January 2026 (3 million+ pages) under the Epstein Files Transparency Act
entries.note: The January 2026 tranche included an apparent diary and emails alleging abuse by Leon Black, which he denies; he told the House Oversight Committee in June 2026 that Epstein "duped" him and sued the committee in September 2026 over a further subpoena. The files also document Epstein's financial ties to the Dubins (Bloomberg, February 2026).

entries.name: Strike MoMA (2021)
entries.note: Followed a letter from 150+ artists demanding Black's removal. Named five trustees: Black, Dubin, Tananbaum, Cohen and Fink. The Guerrilla Girls ran an ad outside the museum targeting the Epstein-linked trustees.

entries.name: The Rockefeller University
entries.note: A weak link: Epstein joined its board of trustees in 2000 and left after one term. The university is a long-running MoMA corporate member.

entries.name: Guerrilla Girls ad takeover (2019)
entries.note: Called for Leon Black and Glenn Dubin to be removed from the board and for their galleries to be draped in black. MoMA did not comment.

entries.name: Climate occupation (Sept 2023)
entries.role: Sit-in that shut MoMA for more than five hours, 17 September 2023
entries.note: At least 16 climate activists were arrested. The target was Henry Kravis, KKR co-founder, over KKR's fossil-fuel holdings; Marie-Josée Kravis chairs the board. Held during the 75,000-strong March to End Fossil Fuels.

entries.name: Palestine occupation (Feb 2024)
entries.role: About 500 protesters filled the atrium and shut the galleries, 10 February 2024
entries.note: Protesters handed out mock pamphlets naming trustees' investments in Israeli weapons makers; more than 100 cultural workers signed a letter on institutional silence over Gaza.

groups.title: Other institutions the same funders pay for

entries.name: Seven other institutions Griffin funds
entries.role: From the atlas study of shared funders
entries.note: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts; M+, Hong Kong; National Gallery, London; National Gallery Singapore; Pérez Art Museum Miami; The Bass, Miami Beach; Whitney Museum of American Art.

entries.name: Four other institutions Black funds
entries.role: From the atlas study of shared funders
entries.note: Bard College; Black Family Visual Arts Center, Dartmouth; Poetry in America, Harvard; Neue Galerie New York.

entries.name: Leaving it on the table
entries.role: Who pays for the cultural spaces on the atlas
entries.note: MoMA is one pin there, flagged for Epstein links, campaigned names and protest. Only Griffin and Black turn up as MoMA funders at other atlas institutions.

groups.title: Historical: the Rockefellers and the Cold War

entries.name: David Rockefeller
entries.note: The David Rockefeller Award, MoMA's main corporate honor, is named for him. Chase Manhattan chairman; Council on Foreign Relations chairman.

entries.name: Rockefeller Brothers Fund
entries.note: The family fund paid $125,000 a year to launch the program that sent Abstract Expressionism abroad.

entries.name: Nelson A. Rockefeller
entries.role: MoMA President (1939–41, 1946–53); NY Governor; US Vice President
entries.note: Ran the wartime Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, then was Assistant Secretary of State (1944–45) and Eisenhower's Special Assistant for Cold War strategy (1954–55), chairing the Planning Coordination Group that oversaw CIA covert operations. Called Abstract Expressionism "free enterprise painting".

entries.name: Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs
entries.note: MoMA was "a minor war contractor": 38 contracts for cultural materials with the Library of Congress, the Office of War Information and above all Rockefeller's CIAA, including 19 exhibitions of American painting shipped around Latin America (Lynes, cited by Cockcroft 1974).

entries.name: René d'Harnoncourt
entries.note: Acting head of the CIAA Art Section (1943–44) and member of the State Department's Advisory Committee on Art before Rockefeller brought him to MoMA in 1944.

entries.name: Porter McCray
entries.note: Worked at the CIAA during the war; entered the Rockefeller orbit through architect Wallace Harrison.

entries.name: MoMA International Program
entries.note: Sent "The New American Painting" (1958–59) through eight European countries and owned the US pavilion at the Venice Biennale (1954–62), the only privately owned national pavilion. The International Council formed in 1953 to support it.

entries.name: Thomas W. Braden
entries.note: Then director of the CIA's International Organizations Division (1951–54). His 1967 Saturday Evening Post piece "I'm Glad the CIA Is 'Immoral'" described the covert cultural program.

entries.name: CIA International Organizations Division
entries.money: ~$900,000 a year to the Congress for Cultural Freedom
entries.note: Documented: the division Braden ran paid for the CCF. Not documented: any direct CIA money to MoMA. Saunders (1999) and Kimmelman (1994) both say the MoMA link was people and shared aims, not funding.

entries.name: Congress for Cultural Freedom
entries.note: Its 1952 Paris festival "Masterpieces of the Twentieth Century" was underwritten by the Farfield Foundation and drew works from MoMA's collection, curated by former MoMA curator James Johnson Sweeney.

entries.name: Farfield Foundation
entries.note: The agency's main pass-through for the CCF. Its president, Julius Fleischmann, sat on the board of MoMA's International Program; MoMA president William Burden is also described as a Farfield president.

entries.name: William A. M. Burden
entries.note: Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Air (1943–47), Air Force special assistant for R&D (1950–52), Ambassador to Belgium (1959–61). Described by Saunders and CounterPunch as a president of the Farfield Foundation; the president on the record is Julius Fleischmann. Announced MoMA's purchase of the Venice pavilion in 1954.

entries.name: Julius Fleischmann
entries.role: Member of the board of MoMA's International Program
entries.note: Cincinnati yeast heir; president of the Farfield Foundation, the CIA's pass-through for the Congress for Cultural Freedom (Saunders 1999).

entries.name: US Information Agency
entries.role: Circulated MoMA's "The Family of Man" abroad, 1955–63
entries.note: MoMA handed Steichen's 503-photograph exhibition to the USIA after its 1955 run; the agency funded and routed it through 37 countries on six continents for eight years, to more than 9 million visitors. A USIS officer in London also helped place MoMA's 1956 Tate show.

entries.name: MoMA Film Library (Iris Barry)
entries.note: Under its CIAA contract the Film Library produced and re-edited documentaries for Latin America and prepared abridged Nazi propaganda films for study groups.

entries.name: Luis Buñuel
entries.note: Hired through the CIAA contract to supervise anti-fascist films for Latin America; dismissed in 1943 after Dalí's memoir called him an atheist and a man of the left.

entries.name: James Johnson Sweeney
entries.note: Curated the CCF's 1952 Paris exhibition; later ran the Guggenheim.

entries.name: John Hay Whitney
entries.note: OSS officer in WWII; Eisenhower's Ambassador to the UK; publisher of the New York Herald Tribune.

entries.name: Whitney Trust
entries.role: Charitable trust exposed in 1967 as a CIA conduit

entries.name: William S. Paley
entries.role: MoMA President and Chairman; CBS founder

entries.name: Peter G. Peterson
entries.role: Life Trustee (d. 2018); Nixon's Commerce Secretary; Blackstone co-founder
